progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: b01 (bacteria, fungi and viruses; viruses are not cells and multiply only inside host cells; most microbes are harmless); b02 (microbes come from other microbes; Pasteur's dust settling; Koch's pure culture on solid media); b03 (water and food as indirect transmission routes; cholera in drinking water). Year 11 Working Scientifically: independent, dependent and controlled variables; validity, reliability and accuracy; risk assessments. Year 11 Module 1 (or Module 5 B2c): bacteria multiply by splitting. Not assumed: indicator organisms, colony-forming units, serial dilution, the countable range, the CFU calculation, risk groups.

progression.stopsAfter: explaining why water is tested and why authorities use E. coli as an indicator, and what a school total count can and cannot show; stating the aim, the independent, dependent and controlled variables, and what a colony-forming unit is; describing sterile sampling of water and preparing a food sample; describing aseptic technique; explaining and carrying out a serial dilution; spreading 0.1 mL on three plates per dilution, labelling the base, taping the lid and incubating inverted at 25 to 30 °C, never 37 °C; explaining the negative and positive controls; choosing the plate with about 30 to 300 colonies and saying why; calculating CFU per mL; stating what colonies can and cannot show; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing the risk assessment (risk group 1, sealed plates never opened, autoclaving before disposal); calculating CFU per mL from new data and fixing a flawed method.

teaching.task: A student's plates show three colonies from tap water, two hundred and fourteen from a creek, and none from a rainwater tank. Is the tank water safe, and is the creek full of disease? How do you design and run a safe, valid test that counts the microbes in a water or food sample, and what can the colonies tell you?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the puzzle (1); (2) contamination is invisible; authorities test for E. coli because it signals faecal contamination; a school total count compares samples but cannot certify safety (2); (3) aim, variables, CFU (3); (4) separate sterile bottles; food as 1 g in 9 mL; aseptic technique keeps outside microbes out (4); (5) dense samples grow a film, so dilute in tenfold steps (5); (6) spread 0.1 mL, three plates each, label the base, tape the lid, incubate inverted at 25 to 30 °C because 37 °C favours microbes adapted to the body (6); (7) the negative control detects added microbes; the positive control shows conditions support growth (7); (8) pick the plate in about 30 to 300: above, colonies merge and the count runs low; below, chance matters too much (8); (9) divide by volume times dilution to scale back (9); (10) colonies show culturable microbes, not pathogens; no colonies does not prove safety (10); VRA (11); risk (12); attempts (13a to 13d); decision rule and handoff (14); key notes (15).
teaching.conversationalApproach: three plates from tap, creek and tank water grew 3, 214 and no colonies, and neither the tank being safe nor the creek being full of disease follows from them, so the practical asks how to count microbes you cannot see and what colonies can and cannot tell you. Contaminated water can look clean; authorities test for E. coli as a sign of faecal contamination, while a school count of everything that grows on nutrient agar compares samples but cannot certify safety. The aim and variables are set with colony forming units per millilitre as the dependent variable; each step is given its reason: separate sterile bottles and aseptic technique, serial dilution in tenfold steps because a crowded plate merges into an uncountable film, three plates per dilution, labelling the base, taping without sealing, incubating upside down at 25 to 30 degrees and never at 37, and a negative and a positive control. One series is read to the plate with about 30 to 300 colonies, scaled back to CFU per millilitre one stage at a time, and the claim is limited to culturable microbes; validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk assessment follow. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: A student plated water from three places. After two days, the tap water plate had three colonies, the creek water plate had two hundred and fourteen, and the rainwater tank plate had none. Is the tank water safe, and is the creek full of disease? Neither follows from these plates. Let's find out.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1, calculate, 3 marks) creek water diluted to 10⁻², 0.1 mL spread on each of three plates, 48 h at 28 °C, 41, 47 and 53 colonies: calculate CFU per mL. Answer: mean 141 ÷ 3 = 47; volume × dilution = 0.1 × 10⁻² = 10⁻³ mL of original sample; 47 ÷ 10⁻³ = 47,000 = 4.7 × 10⁴ CFU per mL. Crossed mistake: "4,700 CFU per mL" (divided by the dilution only, forgetting the 0.1 mL). A1's counts appear nowhere earlier in the video (Revision 2: scene 11's reliability example now uses 150, 156 and 162, mean 156), so the item is unseen. (A2, identify problems and propose improvements, 4 marks) one plate of 1 mL undiluted creek water, 37 °C for 48 h, opened, "too many colonies to count; the creek water contains dangerous bacteria". Answer: any two, each with a fix that removes that problem: undiluted, so colonies merged (serially dilute and count the plate with about 30 to 300 colonies); 37 °C favours microbes adapted to the human body and opening the plate exposed her to whatever grew (incubate at 25 to 30 °C, keep the plate taped and never open it, count through the lid); the conclusion overclaims (colonies show culturable microbes, not pathogens; conclude only that creek water carried many culturable microbes, or test for *E. coli* in an accredited laboratory); one plate with no controls (three plates per dilution and a sterile-water negative control); also accepted (author model, not narrated): 1 mL is too much liquid to spread evenly (spread 0.1 mL). Feedback voices problems one and two and, briefly, the overclaim (the route's stop). Crossed mistake: "repeat it three times" as the fix for the uncountable plate (repeats improve reliability, but three undiluted plates are still uncountable). Owner rule: each improvement must fix the stated problem; the crossed chip models an improvement that does not.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "describe a variety of infectious diseases caused by pathogens, including microorganisms, macroorganisms and non-cellular pathogens, and collect primary and secondary-sourced data and information relating to disease transmission, including: (ACSBL097, ACSBL098, ACSBL116, ACSBL117); design and conduct a practical investigation relating to the microbial testing of water or food samples" this video prepares students to design and run the investigation and to read its results; watching it is not conducting it. It teaches: why water is tested and why authorities test for E. coli (an indicator), against what a school total count can show; the aim and variables; sterile sampling (water, and a food sample made up as a 10⁻¹ suspension); aseptic technique; serial dilution and why it is needed; spreading, labelling, taping and incubating (inverted, 25 to 30 °C, never 37 °C); negative and positive controls; choosing the countable plate (about 30 to 300 colonies); the CFU per mL calculation; what colonies can and cannot show; validity, reliability and accuracy; the risk assessment (risk group 1, AS/NZS 2243.3:2022, sealed plates never reopened, autoclaving before disposal). Placement (playlist order 5): after b03 (order 3) and p01 (order 4), before b04. Not re-taught: pathogen groups and viruses as non-cellular (b01, one clause in scene 10); pure culture and "microbes come from microbes" (b02, one clause in scene 4: the reason lids stay down); water as a transmission route (b03, one clause in scene 2). Not here: identifying species, selective media or E. coli testing as a student method (scene 2: an accredited laboratory's job); antimicrobial discs (p05); outbreak data (g01).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key: water source violet (the independent variable); colonies and CFU amber (the dependent variable); controls green; "culturable microbes" teal and "pathogens" terracotta, kept apart wherever both appear; hazards terracotta; grey for tags and callbacks. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends. All plates on screen are lidded and taped once incubated; no lid lifts after incubation, ever. Reuse: the explainer kit (`Plate`, `Callout`, `Mark`, `Countdown`, `HandText`, `DrawPath`, `scribbleEllipse`, `Enter`); B6a's `WrongChip`, `GreyTag`, `Cross`, `Cam`; bio-m5-p01's method step rail; bio-m6-p01's variables card, VRA cards, risk table layout and colony count grid with tallies (lesson-local there; copy into this lesson's folder or lift to a shared part, root to decide). New coded items (lesson-local): the dilution ladder (coded drops moving 1 mL from tube to tube along the rack plate, each tube gaining a label 10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁴ and a coded "×10" arrow), the plate row (the four aligned dilution plates in a row under their labels, each with a verdict chip), the scale-back line (the formula building term by term: colonies, then volume plated, then dilution, then the product, then the division), and the claim card (two columns, "shows" and "doesn't show"). No human figures.
